hints: A node with no outgoing edges is obviously safe. If all the places a node can go to are safe, is that node safe too?

Work backwards with a reverse graph + Kahn-style peeling: track each node's remaining out-degree; nodes with out-degree 0 are safe. When a node becomes safe, every node pointing to it loses one out-degree. (A white/grey/black DFS also works.)

1. Build reverse edges rev[u] = nodes that point to u, and out[v] = graph[v].length.
  2. Queue every node with out-degree 0.
  3. Pop u, mark safe; for each v in rev[u], decrement out[v], queue it if it hits 0.
  4. Return marked nodes in increasing order.

approaches.name: Brute force
approaches.idea: From each node, DFS all walks and check whether any reaches a cycle.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.idea: Peel safe nodes from the terminals backwards on the reversed graph; nodes on or leading into a cycle never reach out-degree 0.

explain: In the first sample, nodes 5 and 6 have no outgoing edges, so they start in the queue. Removing 5 drops node 2's out-degree to 0 and node 4's to 0, so both become safe. Node 1 still points to 3, and 0→1→3→0 is a cycle, so 0, 1 and 3 never reach 0. The answer is [2,4,5,6]. A self-loop (second sample) keeps a node's out-degree above 0 forever, so it is never safe.
recognize: Nodes whose every path ends at a terminal (cannot reach a cycle) → reverse-graph topological peeling or 3-colour DFS.
